title: Remark
body_md:
Identifying the two binary expansions of each dyadic point, and also
	the endpoints in the circle case, recovers the standard piecewise-linear
	realizations of $\mathsf F$ on $[0,1]$ and $\mathsf T$ on $\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$;
	see \cite{CannonFloydParry1996,CannonFloyd2011}.
head: environment

label: def:smashed
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:smashed}
	The \emph{smashed boundary} is
	\[
	\partial_I^\#\mathcal{F}:=\partial_I\mathcal{F}/\!\sim,
	\qquad
	\varepsilon\sim\eta
	\ \Longleftrightarrow\
	\operatorname{ev}(\varepsilon)=\operatorname{ev}(\eta).
	\]
head: environment

label: def:left-flip
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:left-flip}
On the set of ends of the Farey tree, the \emph{flip at $WL$} is defined as the map
\[
 \phi_{WL}(X)=
 \begin{cases}
  WB^2Y,&X=WBY,\\
  WBAY,&X=WABY,\\
  WAY,&X=WA^2Y,\\
  X,&X\notin\mathcal{C}(W).
 \end{cases}
\]
Its inverse is the \emph{flip at $WL^2$}:
\[
 \phi_{WL^2}(X)=
 \begin{cases}
  WBY,&X=WBBY,\\
  WABY,&X=WBAY,\\
  WAAY,&X=WAY,\\
  X,&X\notin\mathcal{C}(W).
 \end{cases}
\]
head: environment

label: prop:flip-descends
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:flip-descends}
Every flip descends to an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of $\partial_I^{\#}\mathcal{F}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The nontrivial identifications are
	\[
	PAB^\infty\sim PBA^\infty
	\quad(P\text{ admissible}),
	\qquad
	B^\infty\sim SA^\infty,
	\qquad
	A^\infty\sim SB^\infty.
	\]
	The last two pairs represent $0$ and $\infty$, respectively.
	The defining substitutions of each flip and its inverse
	preserve these identifications, so they induce mutually inverse
	homeomorphisms of the quotient.
	
	Within its supporting cylinder, a left flip preserves
	the order of the prefix lists:
	\[
	(WB,WAB,WAA)\longmapsto(WBB,WBA,WA).
	\]
	The base flip cyclically permutes its four initial
	cylinders. Thus every flip preserves cyclic order
	on the quotient.
head: environment

label: def:shuffle
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:shuffle}
On the set of ends of the Farey tree, the \emph{shuffle at $W$} is defined as the local transposition $\sigma_W$ given by
\[
 \sigma_W(WAY)=WBY,\qquad
 \sigma_W(WBY)=WAY,
\]
and $\sigma_W(X)=X$ for $X\notin\mathcal{C}(W)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In fact, the composition
 \[
\bar\kappa\circ\overline{\operatorname{ev}}^{-1}:  \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbf{R})\longrightarrow\mathcal B_{\mathrm{circ}}
 \]
 is the circular Minkowski question-mark function; it sends rational points
 to dyadic points.
head: environment
name: Question-mark conjugacy

label: thm:flip-conjugacy
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:phi-L-binary
title: Proof
body_md:
The flip $\phi_I$ acts by
	\[
	 00 \xi \mapsto01\xi\mapsto 10\xi\mapsto 11\xi \mapsto00\xi.
	\]
	Taking $W=I$ in \cref{def:left-flip} gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-L-binary}
		\phi_L:
		\quad
		00\xi\mapsto000\xi,\qquad
		010\xi\mapsto001\xi,\qquad
		011\xi\mapsto01\xi,
		\qquad 1\xi\mapsto1\xi.
	\end{equation}
	Thus $\phi_L$ is supported on $0\mathcal B$.  Taking $W=S$ gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-SL-binary}
		\phi_{SL}:
		\quad
		0\xi\mapsto0\xi,\qquad
		10\xi\mapsto100\xi,\qquad
		110\xi\mapsto101\xi,\qquad
		111\xi\mapsto11\xi.
	\end{equation}
	Its inverse is the right flip
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-SL2-binary}
		\phi_{SL^2}:
		\quad
		0\xi\mapsto0\xi,\qquad
		100\xi\mapsto10\xi,\qquad
		101\xi\mapsto110\xi,\qquad
		11\xi\mapsto111\xi.
	\end{equation}
	More generally, every flip has a cyclic-order-preserving prefix table, so we deduce $G_{\mathrm{flip}}\leq\mathsf T$.  For the reverse
	inclusion, we calculate the standard generators in flip coordinates. Indeed, $X_1=\phi_{SL}$, $\phi_I^2$ exchanges $0\xi$ and $1\xi$, and hence
	$Y=\phi_I^2$.  Finally, composing this four-cycle with the right-flip table \eqref{eq:phi-SL2-binary}, from right to left, gives
	\[
		 \phi_I\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I^3\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I^3:
		 \quad
		 0\xi\mapsto00\xi,\qquad
		 10\xi\mapsto01\xi,\qquad
		 11\xi\mapsto1\xi.
	\]
	This is the defining table of $X_0$.  Thus the generators in \eqref{eq:FT-generators} belong to $G_{\mathrm{flip}}$, proving the reverse
	inclusion.

label: thm:flip-shuffle-V
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Flip--shuffle realization

title: Proof
body_md:
Under $\kappa$, every flip and shuffle is a finite
	prefix replacement, giving the inclusion in $\mathsf V$.
	Conversely, $\mathsf V=\langle\mathsf T,Z\rangle$,
	where $Z$ exchanges $10\mathcal B$ and $11\mathcal B$
	by prefix replacement and fixes $0\mathcal B$;
	see \cite[\S\S4--6]{CannonFloydParry1996}.
	By \cref{def:shuffle}, $Z=\sigma_S$, while
	\cref{thm:flip-conjugacy} identifies $\mathsf T$
	with $G_{\mathrm{flip}}$. This proves the reverse
	inclusion.
head: environment

label: prop:flip-shuffle-relations
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Local relation families

title: Proof
body_md:
All the relations are verified directly from their definitions. Disjointly supported maps commute.  The
	flip $\phi_{UL}$ carries the supporting prefixes
	\[
	UBR,\qquad UABR,\qquad UAAR
	\]
	respectively to
	\[
	UBBR,\qquad UBAR,\qquad UAR,
	\]
	which proves both the flip transport relations
	\eqref{eq:flip-transport-B}--\eqref{eq:flip-transport-AA} and their mixed
	counterparts
	\eqref{eq:mixed-flip-transport-B}--\eqref{eq:mixed-flip-transport-AA}.
	The shuffle $\sigma_U$ interchanges the prefixes $UBR$ and $UAR$, giving
	\eqref{eq:shuffle-transport} and
	\eqref{eq:mixed-shuffle-transport}.  Finally, refining the relevant prefix
	codes and comparing the substitutions on each cylinder gives
	\eqref{eq:flip-pentagon} and \eqref{eq:flip-shuffle-hexagon}.  Thus every
	displayed identity follows on $\mathcal{C}(U)$, and both sides are the identity
	outside that cylinder.
head: environment

label: lem:effective-finite-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:effective-finite-support}
From a cyclic prefix table for $t\in\mathsf T$, one can compute the marked
edge $\vec e_t$ and the two finite sets
\[
 \mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0,
 \qquad
 \mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t,
\]
and hence $\operatorname{Def}(t)$.  If the table has $n$ entries and size
$s=s(P,Q)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect-table-bound}
 \bigl|\mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0\bigr|\leq n-1,
 \qquad
 \bigl|\mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t\bigr|\leq n-1,
 \qquad
 |\operatorname{Def}(t)|\leq2(n-1)\leq2s.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $t=h_{P,Q,\tau}$. If the table has one row, then $t=1$,
	so the defect is empty and $\vec e_t=\vec e_0$.
	Assume henceforth that $n\geq2$.
	
	For $R=P$ or $R=Q$, let
	\[
	\operatorname{Int}^*(R)
	:=
	\{u\in\{0,1\}^{*}:
	u\ne\varnothing,\ 
	u\text{ is a proper prefix of some }r\in R\}.
	\]
	For each such $u$, let $\widehat u$ be its admissible Farey
	prefix, and put
	\[
	\mathscr A(R)
	:=
	\{\alpha_I\}\cup
	\{\alpha_{\widehat u}:u\in\operatorname{Int}^*(R)\}.
	\]
	A maximal prefix code with $n$ words is obtained from
	$\{\varnothing\}$ by $n-1$ cylinder splittings.  Exactly one
	splitting occurs at the empty prefix, so
	\[
	|\operatorname{Int}^*(R)|=n-2,
	\qquad
	|\mathscr A(R)|\leq n-1.
	\]
	
	Every standard boundary pair outside $\mathscr A(P)$ lies in
	the closed Farey arc associated with a word of $P$.
	On that arc, $t$ agrees with an element of $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$, by
	\eqref{eq:prefix-projective}, and hence maps the pair to a
	standard boundary pair. Consequently,
	\[
	\mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0
	=
	\{t(\alpha):\alpha\in\mathscr A(P),\
	t(\alpha)\notin\mathscr E_0\}.
	\]
	Applying the same argument to
	$t^{-1}=h_{Q,P,\tau^{-1}}$ gives
	\[
	\mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t
	=
	\{\beta\in\mathscr A(Q):
	t^{-1}(\beta)\notin\mathscr E_0\}.
	\]
	These finite sets are computable: evaluate their endpoints
	using the prefix tables and continued-fraction coordinates,
	and test the Farey condition on primitive integer
	representatives. Their cardinalities are each at most $n-1$,
	which proves \eqref{eq:defect-table-bound}.
	
	Finally, the table computes $t(\infty)$ and $t(0)$, and hence
	the marked edge
	\[
	\vec e_t=(t(\infty),t(0)).
	\]
head: environment

label: lem:finite-block-decomposition
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-block-decomposition}
	We have:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\mathscr E[C_K]$ and $\mathscr F[C_K]$ are maximal pairwise
		unlinked families of internal pairs of $C_K$;		
		\item $\mathscr E[C_K]\cap\mathscr F[C_K]=\varnothing$;
		
		\item the finite differences decompose as
		\[
		\mathscr E\setminus\mathscr F
		=
		\bigsqcup_K\mathscr E[C_K],
		\qquad
		\mathscr F\setminus\mathscr E
		=
		\bigsqcup_K\mathscr F[C_K].
		\]
	\end{enumerate}
	
	In particular,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect-cardinalities-equal}
		|\mathscr E\setminus\mathscr F|
		=
		|\mathscr F\setminus\mathscr E|
		=
		\sum_K\bigl(|C_K|-3\bigr).
	\end{equation}
	The decomposition can be computed from the finite symmetric difference and
	the common-neighbour relation.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K$ have $k$ edges.  By construction, the internal members of
	$\mathscr E$ in $C_K$ are precisely the labels of the edges of $K$.
	Therefore
	\[
	|\mathscr E[C_K]|=k=|C_K|-3.
	\]
	In particular, the families $\mathscr E[C_K]$ partition
	$\mathscr E\setminus\mathscr F$.
	
	There is no pair belonging to both $\mathscr E[C_K]$ and $\mathscr F[C_K]$: a common internal pair would be an internal member of $\mathscr E$, hence a label of $K$, hence not in $\mathscr F$.
		
	Let $f\in\mathscr F\setminus\mathscr E$.  By maximality of $\mathscr E$,
	the pair $f$ is linked with some $e\in\mathscr E$.  Since $f$ is unlinked
	with every member of $\mathscr F$, the pair $e$ cannot belong to
	$\mathscr F$.  Hence
	\[
	e\in\mathscr E\setminus\mathscr F.
	\]
	Let $K$ be the component containing the edge labelled by $e$.  Every member
	of $\partial K$ belongs to $\mathscr F$, so $f$ is unlinked with
	$\partial K$.  Since $f$ is linked with an internal pair of $C_K$, the
	cyclic order implies that $f$ is itself internal in $C_K$.  Moreover, $f$ is internal in no other block $C_{K'}$: the pair $e$ is not internal in $C_{K'}$, since the internal members of $\mathscr E$ in $C_{K'}$ are the labels of $K'$, and $e$ is unlinked with $\partial K'$; hence $e$ is unlinked with every internal pair of $C_{K'}$.  Since also $\mathscr F[C_K]\cap\mathscr E\subseteq\mathscr E[C_K]\cap\mathscr F[C_K]=\varnothing$, the families $\mathscr F[C_K]$ partition $\mathscr F\setminus\mathscr E$.
	
                                                                          
                                                                        
                                                                                       
                                                                            
                                                                          
  
	
	Both restrictions are maximal among pairwise unlinked internal
	pairs of $C_K$.  Indeed, let
	$\mathscr H\in\{\mathscr E,\mathscr F\}$.
	Since $\partial K\subseteq\mathscr H$, a member of $\mathscr H$
	linked with an internal pair of $C_K$ must itself be internal
	in $C_K$.  Hence an additional internal pair unlinked with
	$\mathscr H[C_K]$ would be unlinked with all of $\mathscr H$,
	contradicting maximality.
	
	Finally, a maximal pairwise unlinked family of internal pairs on $r$
	cyclically ordered points has $r-3$ members.  Indeed, an internal pair
	divides the cyclic list into two shorter lists, and induction gives
	\[
	(r_1-3)+(r_2-3)+1=r-3,
	\qquad r_1+r_2=r+2.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	|\mathscr E[C_K]|
	=
	|\mathscr F[C_K]|
	=
	|C_K|-3.
	\]
	Summing over the components proves
	\eqref{eq:defect-cardinalities-equal}.
head: environment

label: lem:exchange-flip
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exchange-flip}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $g\in\mathsf T$, $\mathscr E$ is a Farey-type boundary pattern and
		$e\in\mathscr E$, then $g(\mathscr E)$ is a Farey-type boundary pattern and
		\[
		g\bigl(D_e(\mathscr E)\bigr)=D_{g(e)}\bigl(g(\mathscr E)\bigr).
		\]
		\item Every $e\in\mathscr E_0\setminus\{\alpha_I\}$ equals $\alpha_{UB}$ or $\alpha_{UA}$
		for a unique admissible prefix $U$ and a unique letter.  Put
		\[
		\Phi(e):=
		\begin{cases}
			\phi_I,& e=\alpha_I,\\
			\phi_{UL},& e=\alpha_{UB},\\
			\phi_{UL^2},& e=\alpha_{UA}.
		\end{cases}
		\]
		Then $\Phi(e)(\mathscr E_0)=D_e(\mathscr E_0)$ for every $e\in\mathscr E_0$.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) The map $g$ is a bijection of $\mathscr R$ preserving cyclic order, and so
	is $g^{-1}$.  Hence $g$ preserves linking, maximality and common neighbours,
	and
	$g(\mathscr E)\mathbin\triangle\mathscr E_0\subseteq
	g(\mathscr E\mathbin\triangle\mathscr E_0)\cup
	\bigl(g(\mathscr E_0)\mathbin\triangle\mathscr E_0\bigr)$ is finite.
	
	(2) The group $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$ acts transitively on $\mathscr E_0$, and the stabilizer of
	$\alpha_I=\langle0,\infty\rangle$ is $\{1,S\}$.  Every element of $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$ is $W$
	or $WS$, where the reduced word of $W$ is empty or ends in $S$; such $W$ are
	exactly the admissible prefixes.  Thus $e=\alpha_W$ for an admissible $W$, which
	is unique unless $W\in\{I,S\}$, that is, unless $e=\alpha_I$.  For
	$e\neq\alpha_I$, deleting the last turn of $W$ gives the unique $U$ and letter
	with $W\in\{UB,UA\}$.
	
	By \eqref{eq:prefix-projective}, $\phi_L$ maps the closed arcs $[0,1]$, $[1,2]$,
	$[2,\infty]$ onto $[0,\frac12]$, $[\frac12,1]$, $[1,\infty]$ by elements of
	$\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$, and fixes $[\infty,0]$ pointwise.  A standard pair is unlinked with the
	standard pairs bounding these arcs.  Hence it lies in one arc, and is then
	mapped to a standard pair, or it joins two of the breakpoints $0,1,2,\infty$.
	The only standard pair of the second kind bounding no arc is
	$\langle1,\infty\rangle$, and
	$\phi_L\langle1,\infty\rangle=\langle\frac12,\infty\rangle\notin\mathscr E_0$.
	The same argument for $\phi_L^{-1}$, with breakpoints $0,\frac12,1,\infty$,
	shows that $\langle0,1\rangle$ is the only standard pair whose preimage,
	$\langle0,2\rangle$, is not standard.  Since $\frac12$ and $\infty$ are the
	common neighbours of $0$ and $1$, and $0$ and $2$ are those of $1$ and $\infty$,
	\[
	\phi_L(\mathscr E_0)=D_{\alpha_B}(\mathscr E_0),
	\qquad
	\phi_{L^2}(\mathscr E_0)=\phi_L^{-1}(\mathscr E_0)=D_{\alpha_A}(\mathscr E_0).
	\]
	By \eqref{eq:base-flip}, $\phi_I$ permutes the arcs $[0,1]$, $[1,\infty]$,
	$[\infty,-1]$, $[-1,0]$ cyclically by elements of $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$.  The only standard
	pair joining two breakpoints and bounding no arc is $\langle0,\infty\rangle$,
	and $\phi_I^{\pm1}\langle0,\infty\rangle=\langle-1,1\rangle\notin\mathscr E_0$.
	Hence $\phi_I(\mathscr E_0)=D_{\alpha_I}(\mathscr E_0)$.
	
	Finally, let $U$ be admissible.  Left multiplication by $U$ maps $\mathcal{C}(I)$ onto
	$\mathcal{C}(U)$ by $Y\mapsto UY$, so \cref{def:left-flip} gives
	$\phi_{UL}=U\phi_LU^{-1}$ and $\phi_{UL^2}=U\phi_{L^2}U^{-1}$.  Since
	$U(\mathscr E_0)=\mathscr E_0$, $U(\alpha_B)=\alpha_{UB}$ and
	$U(\alpha_A)=\alpha_{UA}$, part (1) gives
	\[
	\phi_{UL}(\mathscr E_0)=U\bigl(D_{\alpha_B}(\mathscr E_0)\bigr)
	=D_{\alpha_{UB}}(\mathscr E_0),
	\qquad
	\phi_{UL^2}(\mathscr E_0)=D_{\alpha_{UA}}(\mathscr E_0).
	\qedhere
	\]
head: environment

label: lem:block-fan-reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:block-fan-reduction}
	Let $C=(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$, with $r\geq4$, and let $\mathscr M$ be a maximal
	pairwise unlinked family of internal pairs of $C$.  There is a sequence of
	\[
	r-3-d_{\mathscr M}(v_1)
	\]
	diagonal exchanges, all supported inside $C$ and fixing $\partial C$, which
	transforms
	\[
	\mathscr M\cup\partial C
	\]
	into the fan $\mathscr F_C(v_1)$.  In particular, the sequence contains at
	most $r-3$ exchanges.
head: environment
name: Block fan reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
List in cyclic order the points joined to $v_1$ by members of
	$\mathscr M\cup\partial C$.  Suppose that this list does not contain every
	point of $C$ other than $v_1$.  Choose two consecutive members $u,v$ for
	which the interval from $u$ to $v$ not containing $v_1$ contains a point of
	$C$.
	
	The pair $\langle u,v\rangle$ is unlinked with every member of
	$\mathscr M$.  Indeed, a pair linked with $\langle u,v\rangle$ would either
	be linked with one of $\langle v_1,u\rangle$ and
	$\langle v_1,v\rangle$, or would join $v_1$ to a point strictly between
	$u$ and $v$, contradicting the choice of consecutive neighbours.
	Maximality therefore gives
	\[
	\langle u,v\rangle\in\mathscr M.
	\]
	
	One common neighbour of $u$ and $v$ is $v_1$.  Let $z$ be the other.  Then
	$z$ lies in the interval from $u$ to $v$ not containing $v_1$, and
	$\langle v_1,z\rangle$ is not present.  Hence the diagonal exchange
	\[
	\langle u,v\rangle\longmapsto\langle v_1,z\rangle
	\]
	is defined.  It adds one internal pair incident with $v_1$ and removes none
	of the pairs already incident with $v_1$.
	
	Each repetition increases by one the number of internal pairs incident with $v_1$.  The fan contains exactly $r-3$ internal pairs incident with
	$v_1$, so the process terminates after
	\[
	r-3-d_{\mathscr M}(v_1)
	\]
	exchanges.  At termination every nonconsecutive vertex is joined to $v_1$,
	and the resulting family is therefore $\mathscr F_C(v_1)$.
head: environment

label: thm:smashed-boundary-algorithm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:smashed-boundary-algorithm}
	Given a cyclic prefix table of size $s$ for $t\in\mathsf T$, the
	deterministic marked fan reduction has the following properties.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item It computes flips $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_{N(t)}$, each of the form
		$\phi_I$, $\phi_{UL}$ or $\phi_{UL^2}$ with $U$ admissible, and the reduced
		word in $S,L,L^2$ of an element $m_t\in\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$ such that
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:smashed-boundary-algorithm-output}
			t=m_t\,\psi_{N(t)}^{-1}\cdots\psi_1^{-1}.
		\end{equation}
		After substituting the fixed flip words for $S,L,L^2$, the right-hand
		side is a word entirely in left and right boundary flips.
		\item The unmarked fan stage is within a factor two of an optimal
		elementary boundary reduction:
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-factor-two-bound}
			k_-(t)=k_+(t),\qquad
			k_-(t)\leq N_{\min}(t)\leq N(t)
			\leq k_-(t)+k_+(t)=2k_-(t).
		\end{equation}
		\item The complete output contains $O(s)$ flip factors, has explicitly
		encoded length $O(s^2)$, and is computed in $O(s^3)$ time under the
		computational convention above.
	\end{enumerate}
	The output word and the residual element depend only on $t$ and the fixed
	ordering conventions, not on the prefix table chosen to compute them.
head: environment
name: Deterministic Farey-boundary reduction and complexity

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Disagreement blocks.}  By \cref{lem:effective-finite-support}, compute
	$\mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0$ and $\mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t$.
	For $e\in\mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0$, its two common neighbours are
	obtained by applying $t$ to the two standard common neighbours of
	$t^{-1}(e)\in\mathscr E_0$.  Hence \cref{lem:finite-block-decomposition}
	computes the disagreement blocks.  Order the blocks by the $\prec$-least member of
	$\mathscr E_0[C]$. These keys are distinct, since the nonempty
	sets $\mathscr E_0[C]$ partition
	$\mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t$.
	For each block, give its $\prec$-least boundary pair its
	preferred orientation and take its initial endpoint as the fan base. In the
	block fan reduction, whenever there is more than one possible gap between
	consecutive neighbours of the base point, choose the first gap in the cyclic
	order beginning with the preferred boundary pair.  These conventions make every
	choice depend only on $\mathscr E_t$ and the fixed order
	\eqref{eq:farey-edge-order}.
	
	\emph{Fan stage.}  In each block $C$, first use the block fan reduction to
	carry the restriction of $\mathscr E_t$ to the chosen fan.  Apply the same
	construction to the restriction of $\mathscr E_0$, and reverse this second
	sequence.  Every exchange fixes $\partial C$, so it changes no other block and
	no pair outside $C$.  Processing all blocks gives pairs $e_1,\ldots,e_N$, where
	$N=N(t)$, and Farey-type boundary patterns
	\[
	\mathscr E^{(0)}=\mathscr E_t,\qquad
	\mathscr E^{(j)}=D_{e_j}\bigl(\mathscr E^{(j-1)}\bigr)
	\quad(e_j\in\mathscr E^{(j-1)}),\qquad
	\mathscr E^{(N)}=\mathscr E_0.
	\]
	
	\emph{Flips.}  Put $\theta_0:=t$, so that $\theta_0(\mathscr E_0)=\mathscr E^{(0)}$.
	If $\theta_{j-1}\in\mathsf T$ satisfies
	$\theta_{j-1}(\mathscr E_0)=\mathscr E^{(j-1)}$, put
	\[
	e_j^\circ:=\theta_{j-1}^{-1}(e_j)\in\mathscr E_0,\qquad
	\psi_j:=\Phi(e_j^\circ),\qquad
	\theta_j:=\theta_{j-1}\psi_j.
	\]
	By \cref{lem:exchange-flip},
	\[
	\theta_j(\mathscr E_0)
	=\theta_{j-1}\bigl(D_{e_j^\circ}(\mathscr E_0)\bigr)
	=D_{e_j}\bigl(\theta_{j-1}(\mathscr E_0)\bigr)
	=\mathscr E^{(j)}.
	\]
	The endpoints of $e_j^\circ$ are obtained by applying the table of
	$t^{-1}$ and then $\psi_1^{-1},\ldots,\psi_{j-1}^{-1}$ to the
	endpoints of $e_j$.  If $e_j^\circ=\alpha_I$, then $\psi_j=\phi_I$.
	
	Otherwise, write $e_j^\circ=\langle x,y\rangle$.  Each of
	$\bar\kappa(x)$ and $\bar\kappa(y)$ has two eventually constant
	binary representatives.  Among the four choices of one
	representative for each endpoint, choose the pair whose longest
	common prefix has greatest length, and denote that prefix by $w$.
	This maximizing pair is unique.  Indeed, if $W$ is the unique
	admissible prefix with $\alpha_W=e_j^\circ$, and $w_W$ is its
	binary code, the two representatives lying in its cylinder are
	$w_W0^\infty$ and $w_W1^\infty$.  Their longest common prefix is
	$w_W$, whereas every other choice gives a shorter common prefix.
	Thus $w=w_W$.
	
	Translate $w$ into the admissible Farey prefix $W$.  Since
	$e_j^\circ\neq\alpha_I$, uniquely write $W=UB$ or $W=UA$.
	Then \cref{lem:exchange-flip} gives
	\[
	\psi_j=
	\begin{cases}
		\phi_{UL},& W=UB,\\
		\phi_{UL^2},& W=UA.
	\end{cases}
	\]
	This explicitly computes the previously defined
	$\psi_j=\Phi(e_j^\circ)$.
		
	\emph{Residual element.}  The element
	$m_t:=\theta_N=t\psi_1\cdots\psi_N$ satisfies $m_t(\mathscr E_0)=\mathscr E_0$.
	Since the stabilizer of $\mathscr E_0$ in $\mathsf T$ is $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$, we have
	$m_t\in\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$.  Compute $m_t(\vec e_0)=(m_t(\infty),m_t(0))$ by applying
	$\psi_N,\ldots,\psi_1$ and then the table of $t$ to $\infty$ and $0$.  Write
	$m_t(\vec e_0)=\left(\frac ac,\frac bd\right)$, choosing primitive integer
	representatives with $ad-bc=1$.  The matrix
	\[
	M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\operatorname{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}
	\]
	sends $\vec e_0=(\infty,0)$ to $m_t(\vec e_0)$, so, by simple transitivity of
	the $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$-action on oriented Farey edges, its class in $\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}$ is $m_t$.
	Applying the Euclidean algorithm to $M$, followed by reduction using
	$\operatorname{\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{Z})}=\langle S,L\mid S^2=L^3=1\rangle$, produces the reduced free-product
	normal form of $m_t$.  Finally, $t\psi_1\cdots\psi_N=m_t$ gives
	\eqref{eq:smashed-boundary-algorithm-output}, and
	\eqref{eq:modular-generators-as-flips} expresses it entirely in boundary flips.
	
	For a disagreement block $C$ with $r$ points, the two
	fan reductions together use at most $2(r-3)$ exchanges.
	By \eqref{eq:defect-cardinalities-equal},
	\[
	N(t)\leq2\sum_C(|C|-3)=2k_-(t),
	\qquad k_-(t)=k_+(t).
	\]
	Every missing standard pair must be inserted, and each
	exchange inserts only one pair. Hence
	$k_-(t)\leq N_{\min}(t)\leq N(t)$, proving
	\eqref{eq:main-factor-two-bound}.
	
	The fixed ordering conventions determine the exchanges
	from $\mathscr E_t$. Starting with $\theta_0=t$, the
	recursion then determines every $\psi_j$ and $m_t$.
	Thus the output is independent of the input table.
	
	The complete output and running-time bounds follow from
	\eqref{eq:complete-bound-lambda},
	\cref{lem:residual-modular-length,cor:T-input-complexity}
	below.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
One may instead insert missing standard pairs successively.
	Give a missing pair $\alpha$ its preferred orientation
	$(x,y)$. Among the pairs $\langle u,v\rangle\in\mathscr E$
	linked with $\alpha$, with $u\in(x,y)$ and $v\in(y,x)$,
	choose the least $u$ and, among ties, the greatest $v$.
	Any member of $\mathscr E$ linked with $\langle x,u\rangle$
	or $\langle x,v\rangle$ would have its first endpoint
	before $u$, or share $u$ and have its second endpoint
	after $v$, contradicting this choice.
	Maximality therefore makes $x$ a common neighbour of
	$u,v$. If $z$ is their other common neighbour, exchange
	$\langle u,v\rangle$ for $\langle x,z\rangle$.
	This decreases the finite number of pairs linked with
	$\alpha$ by one; repetition inserts $\alpha$ by maximality.
	No standard pair is removed, and the number of nonstandard
	pairs never increases. Starting from $\mathscr E_t$, the
	procedure therefore uses at most $k_-(t)k_+(t)$ exchanges.
head: environment
name: Alternative linked-pair insertion

label: lem:address-growth
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Address growth

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $ud^\infty$, with $d\in\{0,1\}$ and $|u|=\ell(x)$, represent $x$.
	
	(1) In binary coordinates, $\phi_{WL}$ acts on $w\mathcal B$ by
	$w0\xi\mapsto w00\xi$, $w10\xi\mapsto w01\xi$, $w11\xi\mapsto w1\xi$, and
	$\phi_{WL^2}$ is its inverse; both fix the complement of $w\mathcal B$.
	Thus a prefix $p$ is replaced by a prefix $q$ with $|q|\leq|p|+1$.  If
	$|u|\geq|p|$, the image of $ud^\infty$ has a representative $vd^\infty$ with
	$|v|\leq|u|+1$.  If $|u|<|p|$, then $p=ud^{\,|p|-|u|}$, and $ud^\infty$ is
	fixed except for $w10\,0^\infty\mapsto w01\,0^\infty$ and
	$w01\,1^\infty\mapsto w10\,1^\infty$, where $\ell$ grows by one.  The base
	flip $\phi_I^{\pm1}$ replaces prefixes of length $2$ by prefixes of length
	$2$, so $\ell$ grows by at most two.
	
	(2) If $ud^\infty\in p_i\mathcal B$, then $h(ud^\infty)=q_{\tau(i)}vd^\infty$
	with $|v|=\max\{|u|-|p_i|,0\}$.
	
	(3) Write $W=S^\delta C_1\cdots C_k$ with $C_i\in\{A,B\}$, so that
	$|w|=k+1$.  The points $W(0)$ and $W(\infty)$ are represented by $w0^\infty$
	and $w1^\infty$.  Hence $\ell(W(0))$ and $\ell(W(\infty))$ are the lengths of
	$w$ with its terminal $0$'s, respectively $1$'s, removed, and one of them is
	$|w|$.  The reduced word $S^\delta L^{i_1}S\cdots L^{i_k}S$ has $\delta+2k\leq2|w|-1$ letters.
head: environment

label: lem:residual-modular-length
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:residual-modular-length}
	If the input prefix table has size $s=s(P,Q)$, then
	\[
	q\leq 2s+4N(t)+1.
	\]
head: environment
name: Residual modular length

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $\ell(\infty)=1$ and $\ell(0)=0$.  By
	\cref{lem:address-growth}(1),(2), the endpoints of
	$m_t(\vec e_0)=t\psi_1\cdots\psi_{N(t)}(\vec e_0)$ satisfy
	$\ell\leq s+2N(t)+1$.  Write $m_t\in\{W,WS\}$ with $W$ admissible, as in the
	proof of \cref{lem:exchange-flip}; then
	$\alpha_W=\langle m_t(0),m_t(\infty)\rangle$.  By
	\cref{lem:address-growth}(3), the binary code $w$ of $W$ satisfies
	$|w|\leq s+2N(t)+1$, and $W$ has at most $2|w|-1$ letters.  The same bound
	holds for $WS$, which is obtained by deleting the final $S$ of $W$, or equals
	$S$ if $W=I$.  Hence $q\leq2|w|-1\leq2s+4N(t)+1$.
head: environment

label: cor:T-input-complexity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:T-input-complexity}
	For a cyclic prefix table of size $s$, the deterministic marked reduction
	produces $O(s)$ flip factors.  Its explicitly encoded output has length
	$O(s^2)$, and a direct implementation on finite $A$--$B$ prefix words has
	running time $O(s^3)$.
head: environment
name: Input-size complexity

label: eq:complete-linear-table-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:defect-table-bound} and
	\eqref{eq:main-factor-two-bound},
	$N(t)\leq k_-(t)+k_+(t)\leq2s$.
	By \cref{lem:residual-modular-length}, $q\leq10s+1$.
	Hence \eqref{eq:complete-bound-lambda} yields
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-linear-table-bound}
		\Lambda_{\mathsf T}(t)\leq N(t)+5q=O(s).
	\end{equation}
	
	Every point handled during the computation has $\ell=O(s)$.  Indeed, the
	endpoints of the pairs in $\mathscr A(P)\cup\mathscr A(Q)$ from the proof of \cref{lem:effective-finite-support} and their standard common neighbours have $\ell\leq s+1$; by \cref{lem:address-growth}, applying
	$t^{\pm1}$ adds at most $s$, each flip adds at most $2$, and at most
	$N(t)\leq2s$ flips are applied to any point.  By
	\cref{lem:address-growth}(3), every $\psi_j$ has a supporting address of
	length $O(s)$, while the modular part uses only $\phi_I$, $\phi_{SL}$ and
	$\phi_{SL^2}$.  Hence the encoded output length is
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-encoded-output-bound}
		O\bigl(N(t)\,s+q\bigr)=O(s^2).
	\end{equation}
	
	The initial finite-defect computation also takes $O(s^3)$
	time. There are $O(s)$ candidate pairs in $\mathscr A(P)\cup\mathscr A(Q)$, and their endpoints
	and required standard common neighbours have addresses
	of length $O(s)$ and integer coordinates of $O(s)$ bits.
	Each required conversion, Farey-condition test, and
	standard common-neighbour computation takes $O(s^2)$
	time with schoolbook arithmetic.
	
	For the running time, there are $O(s)$ such pairs, defect pairs and
	block incidences, each described by words of length $O(s)$.  Constructing
	and ordering the incidence forest uses $O(s^2)$ comparisons of such words,
	hence $O(s^3)$ time.  The fan stage performs $O(s)$ exchanges, each scanning
	$O(s)$ pairs of its block, which costs $O(s^3)$.  Computing $e_j^\circ$
	applies $t^{-1}$ and at most $j-1$ flips to two points with $\ell=O(s)$,
	each application costing $O(s)$; all pull-backs cost
	$O(N(t)^2s)=O(s^3)$.  Computing $m_t(\vec e_0)$ costs $O(N(t)s)$.  Each turn
	at most doubles the entries of the corresponding matrix, so the Euclidean
	reduction involves integers of $O(s)$ bits and costs $O(s^2)$ with
	schoolbook arithmetic; writing the output costs $O(s^2)$.  Thus the total
	running time is $O(s^3)$, without a unit-cost assumption on long addresses
	or rational boundary points.
head: environment

label: ex:marked-fan-reduction
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:marked-fan-reduction}
	Consider the cyclic prefix table
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
		\text{source}&000&0010&0011&01&1\\ \hline
		\text{target}&100&101&11&00&01
	\end{array}
	\]
	for $t=\phi_{SL}L$.  Its boundary defect is
	\[
	\mathscr E_t\setminus\mathscr E_0
	=\{\langle-2,0\rangle\},
	\qquad
	\mathscr E_0\setminus\mathscr E_t
	=\{\langle-1,\infty\rangle\}.
	\]
	There is one disagreement block, with cyclic list
	$(\infty,-2,-1,0)$. 
	Its $\prec$-least boundary pair is $\langle\infty,0\rangle$, with preferred orientation $(\infty,0)$, so the fan base is $\infty$.
	The fan stage consists of the single exchange
	\[
	e_1=\langle-2,0\rangle
	\longmapsto\langle-1,\infty\rangle.
	\]
	
	To extract its flip, pull back the exchanged pair:
	\[
	e_1^\circ=t^{-1}(e_1)
	=\left\langle\frac12,1\right\rangle
	=\alpha_{BA}.
	\]
	Thus $\psi_1=\phi_{BL^2}$ and
	\[
	m_t=t\psi_1=L.
	\]
	The algorithm therefore returns
	\[
	t=L\phi_{BL}.
	\]
	Substituting \eqref{eq:modular-generators-as-flips} gives a
	word entirely in boundary flips.  In particular, the flip
	recorded by the algorithm is determined by the pulled-back
	pair $e_1^\circ$, not by interpreting the diagonal exchange
	itself as a fixed boundary homeomorphism.
head: environment

label: prop:V-effective-algorithm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{prop:V-effective-algorithm}
Given a finite prefix table for $v\in\mathsf V$, there is a finite algorithm which returns
a finite word in flips and the basic shuffle $\sigma_S$ representing $v$.
Apart from finite permutation sorting and word operations, it invokes
$\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}$ three times.
head: environment
name: Flip--shuffle reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the input table as
\[
 v=h_{P,Q,\tau},\qquad
 P=\{p_1<\cdots<p_n\},\qquad
 Q=\{q_1<\cdots<q_n\},
\]
so that
\[
 v(p_i\xi)=q_{\tau(i)}\xi.
\]
If $n<3$, repeatedly expand the row with lexicographically
least source prefix until the table has three rows.
Henceforth $P,Q,\tau$ and $n$ refer to this expanded table.
This preliminary step increases the input size by at most
an absolute constant.

Use the canonical maximal prefix code
\[
 C_n=\{c_1<\cdots<c_n\},\qquad
 c_j=1^{j-1}0\quad(1\leq j<n),\qquad
 c_n=1^{n-1}.
\]
For example, $C_3=\{0,10,11\}$ and
$C_4=\{0,10,110,111\}$.  Define the cyclic prefix replacements
\[
 a_P(c_i\xi)=p_i\xi, \qquad
 a_Q(c_i\xi)=q_i\xi.
\]
They belong to $\mathsf T$.  Define also the cylinder permutation
\[
 \pi_\tau(c_i\xi)=c_{\tau(i)}\xi.
\]
Evaluation on each $p_i\mathcal B$ gives the factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:V-canonical-factorization}
 v=a_Q\pi_\tau a_P^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Compute
\[
 A_P:=\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}(a_P),\qquad
 A_Q:=\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}(a_Q).
\]

Next let $\rho_n\in\mathsf T$ be the cyclic shift of $C_n$,
\[
 \rho_n(c_i\xi)=c_{i+1}\xi\quad(1\leq i<n),
 \qquad
 \rho_n(c_n\xi)=c_1\xi,
\]
and make the third and final call
\[
 R_n:=\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}(\rho_n).
\]
Let $W_n$ be the admissible Farey prefix whose binary code is
$1^{n-2}$; in particular, $W_3=S$.  The shuffle
\[
 z_n:=\sigma_{W_n}
\]
exchanges the last two cylinders
$c_{n-1}\mathcal B$ and $c_n\mathcal B$ and fixes all other cylinders of
$C_n$.  It can be written using only the basic shuffle $\sigma_S$.  Indeed,
$X_0^{-(n-3)}$ sends $10\mathcal B$ and $11\mathcal B$ to those last two
cylinders, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-last-shuffle}
 z_n=X_0^{-(n-3)}\sigma_SX_0^{n-3}.
\end{equation}
Here $X_0$ is already the explicit flip word in
\eqref{eq:flip-generators}.

Let $s_i=(i\ i+1)$ for $1\leq i<n$, acting on the cylinders of $C_n$, and
choose the representative $k_i\in\mathbf{Z}$ of least absolute value satisfying
\[
 k_i\equiv i-(n-1)\pmod n.
\]
If the two representatives have the same absolute value, choose the
nonnegative one.  Thus $2|k_i|\leq n$.
Conjugating \eqref{eq:canonical-last-shuffle} by the appropriate cyclic
shift gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-adjacent-transposition}
 s_i=\rho_n^{k_i}z_n\rho_n^{-k_i}.
\end{equation}

Finally, use bubble sort to write
\[
 \tau=s_{i_r}\cdots s_{i_1}.
\]
Here $r=\operatorname{inv}(\tau)\leq n(n-1)/2$.  Equations
\eqref{eq:canonical-last-shuffle} and
\eqref{eq:canonical-adjacent-transposition} give the explicit word
\begin{equation}\label{eq:V-algorithm-output}
 \boxed{
 \begin{aligned}
 v={}&A_Q
 \bigl(R_n^{k_{i_r}}z_nR_n^{-k_{i_r}}\bigr)
 \cdots
 \bigl(R_n^{k_{i_1}}z_nR_n^{-k_{i_1}}\bigr)
 A_P^{-1},\\
 z_n={}&X_0^{-(n-3)}\sigma_SX_0^{n-3}.
 \end{aligned}}
\end{equation}
Every symbol on the right side is now a flip or the shuffle $\sigma_S$.
The factorization \eqref{eq:V-canonical-factorization} proves correctness,
and termination follows from the termination of
$\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}$ and the finiteness of the sorting procedure.
The use of finite cylinder permutations is standard in the prefix-code
description of $\mathsf V$; see
\cite[\S6]{CannonFloydParry1996} and
\cite[\S2.1]{BleakQuick2017}.
head: environment

label: prop:V-complete-complexity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:V-complete-complexity}
	Let $r=\operatorname{inv}(\tau)$.
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[\textup{(i)}] \emph{Output bound.} The word produced by the
		flip--shuffle reduction satisfies
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:V-complete-length-bound}
			\Lambda_{\mathsf V}(v)
			\leq
			\Lambda_{\mathsf T}(a_P)+\Lambda_{\mathsf T}(a_Q)
			+r\bigl(
			n\Lambda_{\mathsf T}(\rho_n)+10(n-3)+1
			\bigr).
		\end{equation}
		Consequently,
		\[
		\Lambda_{\mathsf V}(v)=O(s_{\mathsf V}^{5}).
		\]
		If every supporting address is written explicitly, the encoded output
		length is $O(s_{\mathsf V}^{7})$.
		
		\item[\textup{(ii)}] \emph{Running time.} A direct implementation which
		writes the fully expanded output runs in
		\[
		O(s_{\mathsf V}^{7})
		\]
		time.  In particular, the flip--shuffle reduction is polynomial-time.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Complete output and running time for $\mathsf V$

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{(i)}
	The word for $X_0$ has five flip factors, so
	$z_n=X_0^{-(n-3)}\sigma_SX_0^{n-3}$ has
	$10(n-3)+1$ factors. Since $2|k_i|\leq n$, each
	adjacent transposition contributes at most
	\[
	n\Lambda_{\mathsf T}(\rho_n)+10(n-3)+1
	\]
	factors. Summing over the $r$ transpositions and adding
	the two outside words proves
	\eqref{eq:V-complete-length-bound}.
	
	The total prefix length of $C_n$ is $O(n^2)$.
	Thus the three calls to $\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}$ have
	input size $O(s_{\mathsf V}+n^2)=O(s_{\mathsf V}^2)$.
	By \cref{cor:T-input-complexity}, each returns
	$O(s_{\mathsf V}^2)$ factors and
	$O(s_{\mathsf V}^4)$ encoded symbols.
	Since $r=O(s_{\mathsf V}^2)$ and
	$n=O(s_{\mathsf V})$, the factor bound gives
	$\Lambda_{\mathsf V}(v)=O(s_{\mathsf V}^5)$.
	There are at most $rn=O(s_{\mathsf V}^3)$ copies
	of $R_n$ or its inverse in the expanded word, giving
	encoded length $O(s_{\mathsf V}^7)$; the outside
	words and copies of $z_n$ contribute lower-order terms.
	
	\smallskip
	\emph{(ii)}
	Table construction and permutation sorting take at most
	$O(s_{\mathsf V}^3)$ bit operations. The three calls
	to $\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}$ take $O(s_{\mathsf V}^6)$
	time altogether. Expanding and writing the resulting
	word takes $O(s_{\mathsf V}^7)$ time, which dominates
	the preceding computations.
head: environment

label: rem:dehornoy-geometric-presentation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:dehornoy-geometric-presentation}
	Under the binary coding $B\leftrightarrow0$ and $A\leftrightarrow1$,
	the identities in \cref{prop:flip-shuffle-relations} correspond to
	Dehornoy's associativity and commutativity relations at nonempty
	addresses, with product order reversed to match our composition
	convention. Including the empty-address instances gives his
	presentation of $\mathsf V$
	\cite[Proposition~3.18]{Dehornoy2005}.
	The finite presentation in \cref{thm:V-flip-shuffle-presentation}
	is obtained by an explicit change of generators from the
	Bleak--Quick presentation
	\cite[Theorem~2.1]{BleakQuick2017}.
head: environment

label: thm:T-flip-presentation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:T-flip-presentation}
	Put
	\[
	 \rho:=\phi_I\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I^3\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I,
	 \qquad
	 \omega:=\rho\phi_I.
	\]
	In the free group on $\phi_I$ and $\phi_{SL^2}$, use the abbreviation
	$\phi_{SL}:=(\phi_{SL^2})^{-1}$.
	Then Thompson's group $\mathsf T$ has the finite presentation
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-direct-flip-presentation}
		\mathsf T\cong
		\left\langle
		\phi_I,\phi_{SL^{2}}
		\ \middle|\
		\begin{aligned}
			&\phi_I^4=1,\qquad
			\rho^3=1,\qquad
			\omega^5=1,\\
			&\phi_{SL}
			=\phi_I^2\rho\phi_I\rho\phi_I^2,\\
			&[\rho\phi_I\rho,\phi_{SL}]=1,\\
			&[\rho\phi_I\rho,
			\phi_I^2\rho\phi_{SL}\rho^2\phi_I^2]=1
		\end{aligned}
		\right\rangle .
	\end{equation}
head: environment
name: A presentation of $\mathsf T$ by boundary flips

title: Proof
body_md:
A direct calculation from the prefix tables gives
	\[
	\rho
	=\phi_I\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I^3\phi_{SL^2}\phi_I
	=L^2.
	\]
	Start with the Lochak--Schneps presentation with generators
	$\alpha$ and $\beta$, using the conjugate relator
	$(\beta\alpha)^5=1$; see
	\cite[Theorem~1]{LochakSchneps1997}.  Adjoin a generator
	$\phi_{SL^2}$ subject to
	\[
	(\phi_{SL^2})^{-1}
	=\alpha^2\beta\alpha\beta\alpha^2.
	\]
	The prefix-table identity
	\[
	\beta
	=\alpha\phi_{SL^2}\alpha^{-1}\phi_{SL^2}\alpha
	\]
	then permits the elimination of $\beta$.  Using $\alpha^4=1$, the
	eliminated word is precisely $\rho$, while
	$\beta\alpha$ becomes $\omega$.  The two commutator relators become
	\[
	[\rho\phi_I\rho,\phi_{SL}]=1
	\]
	and
	\[
	[\rho\phi_I\rho,
	\phi_I^2\rho\phi_{SL}\rho^2\phi_I^2]=1.
	\]
	Thus \eqref{eq:T-direct-flip-presentation} is obtained from the
	Lochak--Schneps presentation by Tietze transformations and is therefore
	complete.
head: environment

label: thm:V-flip-shuffle-presentation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:V-flip-shuffle-presentation}
	Thompson's group $\mathsf V$ has a presentation with generators
	\[
	\phi_I,\qquad \phi_{SL^2},\qquad \sigma_S
	\]
	and the following nine relations:
	\begin{align}
		&\phi_I^4=1,\qquad
		\sigma_S^2=1,\qquad
		\beta^3=1,
		\label{eq:V-finite-torsion}\\
		&\gamma^{\alpha\gamma}=\alpha,
		\label{eq:V-finite-conjugacy}\\
		&\gamma
		=\alpha^{\beta\gamma\alpha\gamma\alpha\alpha^{\beta\alpha}}
		\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\gamma\alpha\gamma\alpha
			\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\alpha}},
		\label{eq:V-finite-splitting}\\
		&\left[
		\alpha^{\beta\gamma\alpha\gamma},
		\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\gamma\alpha\gamma
			\alpha^\beta\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\alpha}}
		\right]=1,
		\label{eq:V-finite-commutation-one}\\
		&\left[
		\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\gamma\alpha\gamma},
		\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\gamma\alpha\gamma
			\alpha^\beta\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\alpha}}
		\right]=1,
		\label{eq:V-finite-commutation-two}\\
		&\left[
		\alpha^{\beta\gamma\alpha^{\beta\gamma\alpha}},
		\alpha^{\beta\gamma\alpha\gamma
			\alpha^\beta\alpha^{\beta^{-1}\alpha}}
		\right]=1,
		\label{eq:V-finite-commutation-three}\\
		&\phi_{SL^2}
		=D^{-1}\phi_I D^{-1}\phi_I^{-2}.
		\label{eq:V-finite-flip-recovery}
	\end{align}
head: environment
name: A finite presentation of $\mathsf V$ by boundary flips and shuffles

title: Proof
body_md:
Start with the three-generator, eight-relation presentation
	$\langle a,b,c\mid\mathcal R_{\mathrm{BQ}}\rangle$
	of \cite[Theorem~2.1, equation~(2.3)]{BleakQuick2017}.
	Passing from their right actions to our left-composition convention
	by taking inverse maps, the generators have the following actions:
	$a$ exchanges $00\xi$ and $01\xi$;
	$b$ sends
	\[
	01\xi\longmapsto11\xi\longmapsto10\xi\longmapsto01\xi;
	\]
	and $c$ exchanges $1\xi$ and $00\xi$.
	Each fixes the complement of the indicated cylinders.
	
	Put
	\[
	p=ab^{-1},\qquad
	z=p^2ap^{-2},\qquad
	d=acacp^2,\qquad
	q=d^{-1}pd^{-1}p^{-2}.
	\]
	Direct composition of these prefix replacements gives
	\[
	p=\phi_I,\qquad z=\sigma_S,\qquad
	d=X_0,\qquad q=\phi_{SL^2}.
	\]
	In particular, \eqref{eq:flip-generators} gives $X_0=\rho\phi_I^2=\omega\phi_I$, so $d=\omega p$, with $\omega$ evaluated in $p,q$.
	
	Conversely,
	\[
	a=p^{-2}zp^2,\qquad b=p^{-1}a.
	\]
	The prefix table
	\[
	dp^2d:\quad
	0\xi\mapsto01\xi,\qquad
	10\xi\mapsto1\xi,\qquad
	11\xi\mapsto00\xi
	\]
	also gives
	\[
	c=(dp^2d)\,z\,(dp^2d)^{-1}.
	\]
	Thus $a,b,c$ are precisely the words
	$\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ displayed above.
	
	Adjoin $p,z,q$ to the Bleak--Quick presentation by their defining
	relations. The recovery identities permit the elimination of
	$a,b,c$. Their eight relators become the relations
	\eqref{eq:V-finite-torsion}-- 
	\eqref{eq:V-finite-commutation-three}:
	indeed, $a^2=1$ becomes $z^2=1$, and, using this relation,
	$(ab)^4=1$ becomes $p^4=1$.
	The defining relation for $q$ becomes
	\eqref{eq:V-finite-flip-recovery}, since $d$ becomes $D$.
	These generator additions and eliminations preserve the presented
	group. Hence the nine displayed relations present $\mathsf V$.
